The board will see this chart on Thursday. Three years in one line. What is the story, Marcos?
Three years ago, we used to sell mostly through distributors. Our share was steady, roughly twelve percent, and nothing used to change.
And then? Did your team use to visit the workshops?
No, we did not use to. The distributors did it. Then we started our own program, and that was the turning point. Workshops grew gradually, every quarter.
What about this fall in the middle? The line goes down sharply.
That was a setback. We were changing the price in March, and sales in the south dropped for two months. It was a slowdown, not a crisis.
Did it recover? The board is going to ask me that first.
Yes. It recovered by July, and now it has leveled off at roughly fourteen percent. We used to talk about price. Now the main factor is the visits.

When I have to explain a chart to the board, I do not describe the line point by point. Nobody remembers that. I tell it in three parts. First, how things used to be. Our share used to be steady, our customers used to buy in the same way, and nothing used to surprise us. Second, the turning point. What changed, and when. A new product, a new price, a new team. Third, how things are now, and what the new normal looks like. Before and after, with one clear moment in the middle. If the line has a setback, I do not hide it. I say what the main factor was, how long it lasted, and how we recovered. A board can accept a bad month. What a board cannot accept is a presenter who does not know why the month was bad.

Most presenters use the same two words for every chart. It went up, it went down. The board hears that ten times and stops listening. The shape of the line is part of the story, so give it a name. Did it go up sharply, in one month, or gradually, over a year? Was it steady before the change? After the problem, did it recover quickly or slowly? And at the end, did it keep growing, or did it level off? Those five or six words change the whole message. Sales dropped sharply sounds like an emergency. Sales slowed down for two months and then recovered sounds like a team in control. It is the same data. The difference is the narrative, and the narrative is your job, not the chart's job.

A small coffee company in the south of Brazil is in the news this week, and its story is a good lesson in numbers. For years, the company used to sell almost all of its coffee to supermarkets. Sales were steady, and the margin used to be very low. Two years ago there was a shift. The company started to sell directly to cafes and restaurants. At first it was a setback. Sales dropped sharply for six months, because the supermarkets bought less and the new customers were still small. Many people in the company wanted to go back. The founder said no. Then the numbers recovered, gradually, one cafe at a time. Today, the company sells less coffee than it used to, but it earns almost twice as much on every kilo. Sales have leveled off, and the founder says that is exactly the plan.
